title: Silvercrest Ventures — Stream SLA & Cold-start Investigation
summary: Intro discovery focused on p95 streaming SLAs, cold-start / KV cache behavior on burst traffic, and tradeoffs between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive inference. Agreed next steps include a short benchmark plan, security doc share, and Dedicated sizing estimate.
topics: burst concurrency and steady-state token/sec expectations
cold-start vs warmed-KV cache behavior and prewarming strategies
fallbacks: quantized model variants and cross-region routing
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-10 08:00 PST | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Maya, Carlos, Anya, Devon, Ravi

[00:00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intro from our side then hear about where you are with latency goals and traffic profiles
[00:00:10] Anya Brooks: thanks Maya, i'll kick off — silvercrest is building a live financial insights feed, low latency is pretty critical, especially for our trader UI. We're aiming for p95 under 200ms for streaming tokens end-to-end, ideally 100–150ms if possible.
[00:00:26] Devon Li: hi, devon here — mostly platform questions: concurrency, autoscaling, how long cold starts take when traffic spikes, and how caching behaves for multi-tenant request patterns.
[00:00:38] Carlos Nguyen: cool — thanks. can i confirm: when you say p95 150ms, is that per-token emission latency in streaming or total time to first token including network?
[00:00:47] Ravi Menon: good point — we mean client-observed first token after request, so network + compute. our frontend is in us-west, majority of traffic there, occasional spikes to eu-west.
[00:00:00] Maya Patel: got it. quick intro on our side — i'm maya, AE, i'll coordinate and send followups. carlos is our performance SE, he's run the token/sec benchmarks and KV cache tuning.
[00:01:05] Carlos Nguyen: hi all. quick overview: for streaming workloads the big levers are model size, quantization, batch window, and whether you're warming KV cache. A warmed KV gives near-linear token throughput; cold starts can add a 100–400ms penalty depending on model.
[00:01:22] Anya Brooks: that's a bit higher than we anticipated. we were hoping cold spikes wouldn't be more than 100ms. what's causing the variance?
[00:01:30] Carlos Nguyen: couple things: first token path includes tokenizer and initial KV generation, and on some model runtimes the kernel selection and memory sync add jitter. second, concurrent bursts can push scheduling onto different GPU slices which changes latency. we do have prewarm and pinning options on Dedicated/Private.
[00:01:52] Devon Li: can you explain pinned capacity vs reserved? is that Dedicated? and how does that compare to Hosted fallback?
[00:01:58] Maya Patel: yes — Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for your tenant. pinning can keep a hot warm cache for pinned models to avoid cold KV building during a spike. Hosted can do smart routing and fallbacks but you might hit multi-tenant jitter.
[00:02:13] Ravi Menon: about fallbacks — are you saying we could fallback to a quantized 4-bit variant automatically? how does quality look?
[00:02:20] Carlos Nguyen: we support automatic fallbacks to quantized variants with a configurable policy. quality delta depends on model and prompt; for many retrieval-augmented prompts it's within acceptable tolerances, but we run evals tied to prompt sets. we can show you sample regression numbers.
[00:02:36] Anya Brooks: okay. for our latency SLOs we need an escape hatch: if p95 crosses threshold for more than 10 minutes, we want deterministic behavior — either surge to Dedicated capacity or route to a smaller model. can Redwood do that?
[00:02:48] Maya Patel: yes — we can define an SLA-based policy: scale to reserved pool if available, else fallback to a pre-approved lighter model. we'll document the policy and costs.
[00:03:00] Devon Li: what about token/sec benchmarking? we need a plan to reproduce our peak — roughly 10k tps sustained for 45s with 600 concurrent users. that's a lot.
[00:03:09] Carlos Nguyen: can you confirm tokens per request and average response length? that changes batching behavior.
[00:03:14] Anya Brooks: average 220 tokens per response, sometimes up to 800 for deep context threads. front-end streams as tokens arrive.
[00:03:22] Carlos Nguyen: ok so long tail responses — that increases per-connection GPU cache usage. for 600 concurrent with 220 tokens avg you are looking at steady-state throughput of ~132k tokens/sec — can we validate that number? might be off if I'm misreading concurrency semantics.
[00:03:37] Ravi Menon: i think that math is right. peak burst could be 200–300% of that for special market events.
[00:03:44] Maya Patel: good to flag burst multipliers. you mentioned multi-region — are you planning active-active or passive failover?
[00:03:51] Anya Brooks: passive failover initially, maybe active-active later. most traffic in us-west. data residency: EU only for some clients.
[00:03:59] Carlos Nguyen: noted. that affects routing latency and required replication of warmed caches in region. you can keep both Dedicated pools and have cross-region warmers but that's more cost.
[00:04:11] Devon Li: about cold-starts — can you prewarm KV for a time window? like before market opens run a prewarm script?
[00:04:18] Carlos Nguyen: absolutely. we have a prewarm API you can call during your window. it pins KV into GPU memory for selected model versions. on Hosted this is available as a paid addon; Dedicated & Private can schedule it as part of tenant policies.
[00:04:30] Anya Brooks: what's the typical duration and cost to keep a model KV warm?
[00:04:34] Carlos Nguyen: depends on model size and GPU memory. e.g., for a 30B model keeping KV warm on a single Dedicated instance might be equivalent to a steady hourly OPEX that we'll estimate in the sizing. rough rule: prewarming reduces cold penalty to <50ms but costs roughly like maintaining 0.2–0.5 x GPU hour for very large models per warm instance. we'll put precise numbers in the followup.
[00:04:56] Devon Li: curious about measurement — if we run benchmarks, what artifacts will you provide? raw latency histograms, token emission traces, kernel-level traces?
[00:05:04] Carlos Nguyen: we'll share per-request traces, p50/p95/p99 histograms, token emit timelines, and a short runbook explaining environment and configs. if you want kernel traces we can capture them for a focused test.
[00:05:16] Ravi Menon: security checklist — SSO, SAML, audit logs, KMS for fine-grained key control, and SOC2 are must-haves. for Private we need on-prem options and HSM integration.
[00:05:26] Maya Patel: we support SAML/SSO, role-based access, audit logs, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS). Private on-prem with HSM is available under enterprise licensing. we'll share our security pack.
[00:05:36] Anya Brooks: any customers doing similar low-latency streaming? curious about real results not just slides.
[00:05:41] Carlos Nguyen: yes — trading and realtime analytics customers have run p95 in the 70–180ms range for streaming first-token when using Dedicated with pinned warmers and optimized batching. Hosted customers hit ~200–350ms in high multi-tenant burst scenarios.
[00:05:56] Devon Li: do you instrument client-side to measure true end-to-end?
[00:05:59] Carlos Nguyen: we instrument both edges — we can provide SDK hooks to capture client-observed TTF (time to first token) and correlate with server traces.
[00:06:07] Anya Brooks: let's talk about the benchmark plan — we want to validate cold start, warmed steady-state, and fallback behavior. can you propose a concise test matrix?
[00:06:15] Carlos Nguyen: propose 3 scenarios: 1) Cold-start burst: ramp 0→600 connections over 20s, measure first-token p95; 2) Warmed steady-state: prewarm KV then run 10k tps for 60s; 3) Fallback failover: induce a synthetic degradation and verify automatic model fallback and throughput retention. we'll provide automation scripts and a short dataset and instrumented client.
[00:06:38] Maya Patel: perfect. we'll also add a policy test: simulate 15 minutes of p95 exceedance and verify scaling to Dedicated/alerting.
[00:06:47] Devon Li: timeline? we want results before our Q1 production release window in late Jan.
[00:06:53] Maya Patel: we can run an initial smoke benchmark next week, full run within two weeks. will that work?
[00:06:59] Anya Brooks: that aligns. we'll need pricing for Dedicated + prewarm costs and Hosted fallback unit economics.
[00:07:07] Maya Patel: i'll send a tailored pricing sheet with Dedicated sizing and an estimated prewarm OPEX.
[00:07:12] Ravi Menon: action on security docs too.
[00:07:15] Maya Patel: yes — security pack attached.
[00:07:18] Carlos Nguyen: quick note — monitoring: we recommend per-route dashboards, token-level cost apportionment, and synthetic probes we can ship as a Grafana dashboard.
[00:07:27] Anya Brooks: that would be useful.
[00:07:30] Devon Li: any gotchas for streaming websockets vs HTTP chunked? we use websockets for session affinity.
[00:07:36] Carlos Nguyen: websockets give better affinity and lower rehandshake overhead on long-lived sessions; recommend on Dedicated. Hosted supports both but affinity on multi-tenant may cause you to land on different hosts post-failover. we can document sticky routing choices.
[00:07:53] Maya Patel: quick recap: Redwood—burn down next steps: 1) run smoke benchmark next week; 2) share Dedicated sizing and pricing and prewarm cost estimate; 3) send security pack; 4) provide benchmark scripts and dashboard templates. any other asks?
[00:08:09] Anya Brooks: please include example regression numbers for the quantized fallbacks against our sample prompts.
[00:08:14] Maya Patel: noted. thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmarking window.
[00:08:20] (crosstalk and small talk)
[00:08:30] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll close there.
